section.title: Concluding Exhortations
section.sectionRationale: The doctrine now becomes daily life. The writer gathers practical exhortations: love, hospitality, compassion, pure marriage, contentment. He anchors them in the unchanging Christ and the presence of God, calls believers to go to Jesus outside the camp bearing His disgrace, and to offer the ongoing sacrifices of praise and good works while honouring their leaders.
section.thesis: The finished work of Christ issues in a transformed life: persevering love, hospitality, compassion, faithful marriage, and contentment grounded in God's promise never to forsake His people; and because Jesus Christ is unchanging and suffered outside the camp, believers go out to Him bearing His reproach, seeking the city to come and offering continual sacrifices of praise and good works.
section.frameNote: Three movements: everyday exhortations to love, hospitality, purity, and contentment; the unchanging Christ and the call to go outside the camp seeking the city to come; and the sacrifices of praise and good deeds, with honour and prayer for leaders.

verses.text: Do not neglect to show {{philoxenia|hospitality}} to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it.
Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them.
Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.
Keep your lives {{aphilargyros|free from the love of money}} and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.”
So we say with confidence: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?”

units.label: The unchanging Christ, outside the camp

verses.text: Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them.
We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat.
Although the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin, the bodies are burned outside the camp.
And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood.
Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.
For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.

units.label: Sacrifices of praise, honour your leaders
units.note: the fruit of lips that confess His name

verses.text: Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a {{thysia|sacrifice}} of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.
And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you.
Pray for us; we are convinced that we have a clear conscience and desire to live honorably in every way.
And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon.

philadelphia.gloss: Brotherly love, the affection of family. Believers are one family in Christ, so love among them is to continue and deepen; it heads the list of practical duties as the atmosphere of the whole Christian life.

philoxenia.gloss: Hospitality, literally love of strangers. Welcoming strangers reflects God's welcome of us; the writer recalls that some, like Abraham, unknowingly hosted angels, so hospitality may carry unseen blessing.

aphilargyros.gloss: Free from the love of money, not greedy. Contentment rests not on wealth but on God's promise never to leave or forsake His people, so the believer can be free from money's grip and unafraid.

thysia.gloss: A sacrifice, an offering to God. Since Christ's one sacrifice for sin is complete, the sacrifices believers now offer are those of praise and good works, the fruit of lips confessing His name and lives doing good.

basic.context: After twelve chapters of soaring doctrine, the letter turns to everyday life. Keep loving one another. Welcome strangers. Remember prisoners. Honour marriage. Do not love money, but be content, because God has promised never to forsake you. Then the writer roots it all in the unchanging Christ, calls believers to go to Jesus outside the camp bearing His shame, and to offer the ongoing sacrifices of praise and good deeds.
basic.hermeneutics: Read these as the fruit of the gospel just expounded, not a change of subject. The 'therefore' of verse 15 shows praise and good works flow from Christ's finished sacrifice. 'Outside the camp' connects Jesus' rejection to the believer's willingness to share His reproach.
basic.originalLanguages: Continue in philadelphia, brotherly love; show philoxenia, hospitality; keep life aphilargyros, free from the love of money; and offer the thysia, sacrifice, of praise.
basic.typology: The sin offering whose body was burned outside the camp foreshadows Jesus, who suffered outside the city gate. The believer's going out to Him fulfills the call to leave the old order and follow the rejected Christ.
basic.christ: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, the anchor of a stable life amid strange teachings. He suffered outside the gate to sanctify His people by His blood, and through Him we offer acceptable praise.
basic.god: God promises never to leave nor forsake His people, freeing them from fear and greed. God is the helper we need not fear anyone against, and He is pleased with the sacrifices of praise and generosity.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 31 and Joshua 1 underlie the promise never to forsake. Psalm 118 supplies the Lord is my helper. Leviticus 16 gives the sin offering burned outside the camp.
basic.oneStory: The doctrine of Christ's finished work now shapes a whole way of living: a pilgrim people, loving, generous, and unafraid, following the rejected Christ toward the city that is to come.

context.literary:
Chapter 13 reads like a string of short commands, but they are not scattered. Verses 1 to 6 give five or six brief instructions about relationships, hospitality, prisoners, marriage and money, each one stated in a line or two and then, for the last, backed by a quotation from the Old Testament. Verses 7 to 9 are held together by the idea of what stays the same: the leaders' faith to be imitated, Jesus Christ the same yesterday, today and forever, and the contrast with strange teachings that carry people about. Verses 10 to 16 are the doctrinal heart of the chapter, a compact argument about altar, sacrifice and camp that goes back to the Day of Atonement. Verses 17 to 19 return to the leaders and ask for prayer.

Leaders frame the middle of the chapter. They are mentioned in verse 7, in verse 17 and again in verse 24, always with a word about the community's relationship to them: remember them, obey them, greet them. The statement about Jesus in verse 8 is set between two commands about leaders and teaching, so it works as the anchor of the section: the faith they taught points to a Christ who does not change.

Verses 10 to 14 use the vocabulary of place. Altar, tabernacle, Holy Place, camp, city gate, outside, city: the passage is a map. It moves the reader from the Day of Atonement ritual inside the sanctuary, to the burning of the bodies outside the camp, to Jesus outside the gate, to the call to go to Him there, to the city that is to come. By verse 15 the movement has reached its goal, with the word "therefore" turning from place to praise.

The register has changed from the earlier chapters, but the writer shows it is the same mind. The "therefore" of verse 13 and verse 15 shows that the practical commands are the conclusion of the argument, and the phrase "sacrifices... God is pleased" in verse 16 recalls the sacrificial language of chapters 8 to 10.
context.historical:
The community addressed has already had a hard history. Earlier the writer recalls that they endured a great contest of suffering, public abuse, imprisonment and the seizure of their property, 10:32-34. In 13:3 prisoners and the mistreated are still present among them, so the call to remember them as if bound with them is a call to stand openly with people at real risk.

Hospitality to strangers was a basic social need in a world where travellers depended on private homes, and for the early churches it was how itinerant teachers and refugees survived. The line about entertaining angels without knowing it recalls Abraham and Sarah's welcome of three visitors at Mamre, Genesis 18:1-8, and Lot's guests at Sodom. The first hearers would have heard a very practical verse as well as a story.

The warning about money and marriage reflects the pressures of the age. Marriage was exposed to the freedom of the Roman world's sexual customs, and contentment was hard for people who had lost their goods, which is why the writer reaches back for God's promise to Joshua and Israel: never will I leave you, never will I forsake you. Deuteronomy 31:6 gives the promise to the whole people, and Joshua 1:5 gives it to the new leader.

The strange teachings about foods in verse 9 point to some kind of ritual or dietary teaching that tied spiritual strength to meals. We cannot identify the group with certainty, and the writer does not name it. The language of "camp" in verses 11 to 13 recalls the wilderness years when the whole tabernacle community lived around the tent and the sin offering was burned outside, Leviticus 16:27 and Leviticus 4:12. For Jewish believers, to go outside the camp meant to leave the sacred centre of their national and religious life.
context.canonical:
The chapter is built on four Old Testament pillars. The promise "Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you" in verse 5 echoes Deuteronomy 31:6 and Joshua 1:5, texts that gave the promise at moments of transition, when Israel stood to enter the land and when Joshua took Moses' place. Hebrews makes the old promise the answer to the love of money: if God stays, nothing else is needed.

Verse 6 quotes Psalm 118:6, "The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?", though Hebrews renders the first line "The Lord is my helper." The psalm is a song of thanksgiving sung by the pilgrims going up to the temple, so the writer places believers in the same procession.

Verses 11 and 12 draw on Leviticus 16, the Day of Atonement, in which the blood of the sin offering was brought into the Most Holy Place and the bodies were burned outside the camp, Leviticus 16:27. Leviticus 4:12 describes the same practice for other sin offerings. Hebrews takes a detail that was only a rule about disposal and treats it as a pattern fulfilled when Jesus suffered outside the gate.

The sacrifices of praise in verse 15 build on the Psalms, where thanksgiving is offered as a sacrifice, Psalm 50:14, and on Hosea 14:2, where the people are told to present the fruit of their lips. In Romans 12:1 Paul speaks of living sacrifices, and in Philippians 4:18 of gifts as a fragrant offering, so the idea that sacrifice has moved from altar to life is a New Testament commonplace.

Acts 13:15 uses the same phrase as Hebrews 13:22, the word of exhortation, of a synagogue sermon. It is a clue that the whole letter is a sermon sent in writing.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer is turning doctrine into a way of life, and he wants the readers to see that these ordinary commands are not an appendix. They are what the gospel looks like in practice. People who have been given a kingdom that cannot be shaken have no need to cling, to hoard or to defend themselves, so they are free to love, to open their doors and to stand with the suffering.

The commands are chosen with care. Brotherly love is first because it is the foundation of the community's survival, and it is something already present that must be continued, not started. Hospitality, prison visiting and marriage faithfulness are the three places where love costs something: time, risk and self-control. Contentment is the inner condition that makes these possible, and it rests on a promise rather than on a feeling.

The writer also wants his readers to pay attention to who and what they follow. He asks them to remember their leaders and to imitate their faith, but he roots it in Christ, not in the leaders, so that loyalty to a teacher can never replace loyalty to the one who does not change.

Finally he calls them outside the camp. He wants them to understand that following Christ may cost them their standing in the only community they knew, and to accept that gladly, because the city they belong to has not yet come into view.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is almost entirely prescriptive, which is unusual in Scripture, and so the main work of application is to hear each command at its proper weight. The commands to love, to show hospitality, to remember prisoners and to honour marriage are plain instructions for every Christian, in every age. The command to be content is a command about the heart, not a ban on possessions; verse 5 asks for freedom from the love of money, not for poverty.

Some details are specific to the first readers. The strange teachings about foods belonged to a particular situation, and it would be wrong to read the verse as a rule about modern diets. The call to go outside the camp has an obvious historical form for Jewish Christians, but its principle, readiness to bear Christ's reproach and to hold the world's approval loosely, belongs to every believer.

The line about obeying leaders must be read in context. It is a command to the community and it is balanced by the leaders' accountability: they will give an account, and they are described as watching over souls, not lording it over them. It does not give leaders unlimited authority, and the earlier call in verse 7 to consider the outcome of their lives and imitate their faith shows that the obedience is owed to those whose lives match the word.

debates.question: What is the altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat?

views.label: The cross and the sacrifice of Christ
views.case: Verse 10 sits beside the argument about the sin offering burned outside the camp, so many readers take the altar as the place where Jesus offered Himself. Priests under the old order ate portions of some sacrifices but not of the sin offering whose blood entered the sanctuary, Leviticus 6:30, and the point would be that those who cling to the old system have no share in the benefits of Christ's sacrifice.

views.label: The benefits of Christ received by faith
views.case: Others see the altar as a way of speaking about what believers have in Christ, a spiritual feeding, the grace that strengthens the heart in verse 9. The contrast is then between grace and the food rules of verse 9, not just between altars.

views.label: The Lord's Supper
views.case: Some interpreters have taken the altar to be the Lord's table. The verse does not mention it and the context is about sacrifice and place, so this reading is held more cautiously and is a minority view in modern commentary.

debates.bearing: Whichever way the altar is understood, the point is the same: the old priests have no claim on what Christ has done, and believers have full access. The verse protects the finished work.

debates.question: What does it mean to go 'outside the camp' to Jesus?

views.label: Leave the old covenant system
views.case: For Jewish Christians tempted to return to the synagogue and temple, the call is to break with the old worship and its social safety, bearing the disgrace of being counted as outsiders. This fits the letter's whole purpose.

views.label: Stand with the rejected and share His reproach
views.case: Others stress the moral force of the call, that wherever the world's respectable centre rejects Christ, His people go to Him there and bear what He bore. The camp becomes any system of security that stands against Him.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Many readers hold that the first meaning is historical and the second is its lasting application, which is why verse 14 immediately speaks of the city to come.

debates.bearing: The call is not to withdraw from society or seek suffering but to refuse to anchor identity or safety in anything but Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 begins with philadelphia, love of the brothers, and its command is "let it remain", menetō. The verb is the same one used of the permanent city in verse 14 and of Christ's priesthood that remains, 7:24, which quietly links the stability of love to the stability of God's plan. Verse 2's philoxenia, hospitality, is literally "love of strangers", and the two words share the same prefix, so the writer has put a family word and a stranger word side by side: the community loves its own and the foreigner with the same kind of love. The angels are "entertained", elathon, "they escaped notice", a Greek idiom for doing something without realising.

In verse 3 the writer uses mimnēskesthe, "remember", which often means more than recall; it means to act on what you remember. The prisoners are described as desmioi, "bound ones", and the verb "as if bound with them", sundedemenoi, joins the reader to the prisoner. Verse 4's timios, "honoured", is the same word used of precious things. Verse 5 requires aphilargyros, "without love of silver", literally a character, tropos, free of it, and the word arkoumenoi, "being satisfied", is the content of contentment: to be enough with what you have.

The promise of verse 5 is stacked with Greek negatives, so that the sentence is more emphatic than any English wording can be. God's word to Joshua is thus delivered to the readers as a promise made to them.

Verse 7 calls the leaders hēgoumenoi, "those who lead", the same word used in verse 17 and verse 24. The command to "consider the outcome", anatheōrountes tēn ekbasin, means looking carefully at the result of a life, and "imitate", mimeisthe, is the verb from which we get mimic. In verse 17 the verb peithesthe is "be persuaded" and hypeikete "yield", and the leaders "keep watch", agrypnousin, literally stay awake, over souls.

Verse 15's thysia aineseōs, "sacrifice of praise", is the Greek translation of a Hebrew idea found in the Psalms. The fruit of lips that confess, homologountōn, joins praise to public confession of the name. In verse 16 koinōnia, "sharing", is the same word used of fellowship, so generosity is treated as an act of communion, and God is "pleased", euaresteitai, a word of the same root as the one used in the benediction.

typology.type: The sin offering burned outside the camp
typology.fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement the blood of the sin offering was carried into the Most Holy Place, and the bodies were burned outside the camp, Leviticus 16:27. Hebrews finds in that detail a pattern fulfilled when Jesus suffered outside the city gate, verse 12. The correspondence is of place and purpose: both the animals and Jesus were taken outside, and both were for sin. The escalation is that His blood sanctifies the people, not only the sanctuary, and does so once for all, 10:10. The type falls short because the animals could not make the worshippers perfect, 10:1-4, and because no priest had to go to Christ outside; He came out to them.

typology.type: The camp and the wilderness journey
typology.fulfillment: The wilderness camp, with the tabernacle at its centre, was the shape of Israel's life as a people in transit, and Moses' tent outside the camp was where those who sought the LORD went, Exodus 33:7. The readers are asked to see themselves as that pilgrim people. Abraham and the patriarchs lived as strangers seeking a better country, Hebrews 11:13-16. In Christ the journey has a destination that is not a place on earth, and the pilgrim community is no longer a nation but those who are drawn to Him. The type falls short in that Israel's camp was the centre of the world's only revealed worship; the believer's camp is the city to come.

Israel's daily offerings, Exodus 29:38, were the framework of worship. With Christ's one offering complete, the sacrifices that remain are the fruit of lips and the sharing of goods, which Psalm 50:14 and Hosea 14:2 had already hinted at as what God truly desired. Paul speaks in the same way of bodies as living sacrifices, Romans 12:1, and of gifts as an offering, Philippians 4:18. The pattern is fulfilled in that these are not sacrifices that take away sin, but responses to the One who did. They fall short of the old pattern in that they atone for nothing; they are pleasing to God only because they come through Jesus.

study.christ:
The chapter sets Christ at its centre with a single sentence that is easily read as a slogan: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. In the letter this is more than a comfort. The writer has spent twelve chapters showing that the Son is the radiance of God's glory, that He remains while the heavens wear out, 1:10-12, and that He has an indestructible life, 7:16. His sameness is what makes His sacrifice permanent and His priesthood unchanging. Strange teachings come and go, but the one in whom the faith is anchored does not.

He is also the one who suffered outside the gate. The writer recalls the burning of the sin offering outside the camp and sees in it a picture of the cross. Jesus died outside Jerusalem, as the Gospels record, and so He took on the place of the unclean and the condemned. Yet He did it to sanctify the people by His own blood. The shame and the cleansing belong together. The place that looked like rejection was the place of atonement.

To go to Him outside the camp is therefore to go to the Saviour who already stands there. The believer is not asked to endure disgrace alone; it is "the disgrace He bore", and He bore it first. The call is not to reproduce His sufferings but to follow Him to where He is, and to count His company worth more than the camp's respectability.

Finally, Christ is the one through whom everything in the Christian life is offered. The sacrifice of praise goes up "through Jesus", verse 15. Our generosity and our confession are not pleasing in themselves; they are pleasing because they come through the One who offered Himself, and who, as the great high priest, presents what we bring.

A word of care: the Day of Atonement details are not a code for every part of Jesus' life. The link rests on what the text itself says, that Jesus suffered outside the city gate for the sanctification of the people, and on the earlier chapters' explanation of His blood and His priesthood.
study.god:
In this chapter God is above all the One who stays. The promise of verse 5, never will I leave you, never will I forsake you, was spoken first to a people about to face an enemy and to a leader about to take over. The writer takes it and puts it in the mouth of ordinary believers worried about money. It reveals that God's faithfulness is not a general mood but a promise in particular words, given to be believed in particular fears.

Because He stays, believers can say with confidence, "The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid." The question "What can man do to me?" is not a denial that people can hurt us, since the readers had been imprisoned and robbed. It is a statement that no human act can undo the presence of God. This is how God's attributes shape the doctrine of Christian courage: He is helper because He is present and powerful, and fear loses its hold when those truths are believed.

He is also the Judge of those who defile marriage, verse 4. The writer has not forgotten the serious side of God's holiness from chapter 12, and he places the warning in the middle of ordinary instructions. The God who is a consuming fire is the one who asks for faithfulness in bed and in business, so holiness is not confined to temples.

He is a God who is pleased, verse 16. This is a remarkable thing to say of a God who is also a fire. The text says that with sacrifices of praise and of sharing, God is pleased, and it shows that He receives what is offered through His Son with delight. It tells us that God's character includes a warmth toward the obedience of His children, not merely a demand for it.

He is the God of a city. Verse 14 says believers look for the city to come, and elsewhere the letter says that God has prepared a city for His people, 11:16. God is not a deity attached to a place that can be shaken; He is building a home, and for worship this means we hold lightly what He has not promised to keep, and tightly what He has.

crossReferences.note: Moses tells all Israel that the LORD will never leave them nor forsake them. It is one of the two texts behind verse 5. Read in its setting, it is a promise made to a people who were about to enter a land full of enemies, which is the kind of fear the readers also faced.

The same promise given to Joshua as he replaces Moses. Hebrews uses it to show that God's presence does not depend on a great leader, and that the promise made to Joshua is now made to everyday believers.
The source of the confidence in verse 6. The psalm is a thanksgiving for deliverance, and Hebrews makes its question, what can man do to me, the believers' answer to those who threaten them.

Abraham runs to meet three visitors and offers them water and food, not knowing who they are. This is the story that stands behind the line about entertaining angels. It shows hospitality as an ordinary act that may hold more than it seems.

The bodies of the sin offerings, whose blood had been taken into the Most Holy Place, are carried outside the camp and burned. This is the pattern verse 11 describes, and it is the detail the writer applies to Jesus' death outside the city gate.

The same practice for the sin offering of the priest: the whole bull is taken outside the camp and burned. Together with Leviticus 16, it shows that the burning outside was a regular part of the law of sin offerings, not a one-off.

Moses pitched the Tent of Meeting outside the camp, and anyone inquiring of the LORD went out to it. It shows that outside the camp had once been a place of meeting with God, which softens the sense of exclusion in verse 13.

The patriarchs were strangers and exiles, longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Chapter 13's 'we do not have a permanent city' is the same pilgrim identity, now applied to the readers who are asked to live loosely.

God asks for a thank offering rather than bulls and goats. It shows that praise as sacrifice is an Old Testament idea, so verse 15 is not inventing a new category but reaching for what the psalms had pointed to.

The returning people are told to bring words and present the fruit of their lips. Hebrews 13:15 takes up the very image, 'the fruit of lips that confess His name', and joins it to Jesus as the one through whom the offering is made.

Paul urges believers to offer their bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God. It is the same shift from altar to life, and it shows that Hebrews and Paul agree on how the cross changes worship.

God works in believers to will and to act for His good purpose. It prepares for the benediction, where God is asked to equip His people and to accomplish in them what pleases Him, and it shows that obedience in chapter 13 is also His work.

study.oneStory:
Hebrews 13 is the place where the story's highest doctrine meets everyday life. From Eden, human life was meant to be a life of love toward God and neighbour, lived out in a good world as God's image-bearers. The fall broke that, and the history of Israel is the history of God teaching a people again what that life looks like: hospitality to the stranger, justice for the prisoner, faithfulness in marriage, freedom from covetousness. The Law's commands on all these points lie in the background of the chapter, and Hebrews says that they are now fulfilled through a new heart, not a written code.

The central image of the camp and the city is the story's own geography. Humanity left a garden and walked east, Israel left Egypt and lived in a camp with God at the centre, then settled in a land with Jerusalem at the centre, and was finally sent into exile. The question of where God's people really live runs through all of it. Hebrews answers that the people of Christ live outside the camp, with Him, and that their home is the city that is to come.

That city is promised throughout the Old Testament, in the hope of Abraham, who looked for the city with foundations, 11:10, and in the vision of Zion. Revelation 21:2 sees it coming down from heaven. Until it arrives, God's people are pilgrims, and they live as people who are not afraid of loss because their security is not in the camp.

The sacrifices of praise and sharing also belong to the end of the story. In the new creation there is no temple, Revelation 21:22, because God Himself is the temple; what remains is worship and the sharing of everything in a city where the gates are never shut. Believers rehearse it now. Every act of hospitality and every thank offering is a small preview of the life of the new creation, offered through the Christ who has already gone out to meet us.

quiz.q: What is the basis for being content and free from the love of money?

options.text: God's promise, Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.
options.note: Verse 5 grounds contentment in God's abiding presence.

options.text: Confidence that the Lord is our helper, so we need not fear.
options.note: True, from verse 6, and it rests on God's promise never to leave nor forsake His people.
It is the love of money, not money itself, that is warned against; contentment rests on God's promise.

options.text: The certainty that we will become rich.
options.note: The basis is God's presence, not the hope of riches.

quiz.q: What does 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever' guard against?

options.text: Being carried away by all kinds of strange teachings.
options.note: Verses 8 to 9 link Christ's constancy to steadfastness in truth.

options.text: Ever needing to grow or learn.
options.note: It anchors us in the unchanging Christ, which fuels growth, not stagnation.
It affirms His constancy; He is indeed alive and unchanging.

options.text: Fearing that Christ might change toward us.
options.note: His constancy assures us He will not change toward us, and here it specifically guards against being carried away by strange teachings.

quiz.q: What does it mean to go to Jesus 'outside the camp'?

options.text: To leave the security of the old order and identify with the rejected Christ, bearing His disgrace.
options.note: Verses 12 to 13 call believers to share Christ's reproach.

options.text: To seek the city that is to come rather than a permanent one here.
options.note: This is a true, related emphasis from verse 14, and the immediate call is to go to Jesus outside the camp, bearing His disgrace.
It means sharing Christ's reproach, not isolating from His people.

options.text: To keep to the old tabernacle system.
options.note: It is the opposite: leaving the old system to follow Christ.

quiz.q: What sacrifices do believers now offer through Jesus?

options.text: The sacrifice of praise and the sacrifice of doing good and sharing with others.
options.note: Verses 15 to 16 name these spiritual sacrifices.
Christ's one sacrifice for sin is finished; ours are praise and good works.
We still offer sacrifices, but of praise and generosity, not for sin.

options.text: The sacrifice of praise that confesses His name.
options.note: This is half the answer; the passage also names doing good and sharing with others as sacrifices pleasing to God.

questions: The chapter opens with brotherly love and hospitality. Who is a stranger or outsider you could welcome as Christ has welcomed you?
Contentment is rooted in God's promise never to forsake you. Where is the love of money or fear of lack still gripping your heart?
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. How does His unchanging constancy steady you in a season of change?
We are called to go to Jesus outside the camp, bearing His disgrace. What reproach for Christ are you being asked to accept right now?
God is pleased with sacrifices of praise and good works. What would it look like to make praise and generosity a continual offering this week?

translationNotes.note: 'Hospitality' translates philoxenia, love of strangers; the reference to entertaining angels unawares recalls Abraham and Sarah welcoming visitors in Genesis 18.
The promise 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you' draws on Deuteronomy 31:6, 8 and Joshua 1:5; the Greek piles up negatives for strong emphasis.
'Sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips' echoes Hosea 14:2 and the Psalms; under the new covenant the offering is thanksgiving and confession rather than animal sacrifice.
